idiom_name: if (bad) return code; guards, with goto-chain cleanup when the function owns resources
implementation_notes: C realises the guard with the only control flow it has: an if and an immediate return, with the failure shape following the local convention - an int errno-style status, a NULL pointer, or a caller-owned error struct. The classic single-exit habit is still justified for functions that hold several resources: CERT MEM12-C shows that returning halfway through such a function leaks every resource acquired since the last exit, and its compliant solution routes each guard through a goto chain into an ordered cleanup sequence (goto FAIL_FIN2; ... FAIL_FIN2: fclose(fin2); FAIL_FIN1: fclose(fin1);). Where the function owns nothing yet, the plain early return is the right form - put the argument guards before the first acquisition so no cleanup is needed at all.
pitfalls: Early returns leak when the function owns resources: each exit must release the growing prefix (CERT MEM12-C), which is exactly what the goto-chain variant exists for.
errno is valid only immediately after the failing call and is clobbered by any later library call; save it before returning (the -errno pattern) instead of reading it later.
Return-code conventions (-1 vs -errno vs NULL) must match the caller's checker; a guard that returns 0 or a valid-looking pointer on failure fails open and hides the error.

variants.name: Single-exit guards with an ordered goto cleanup chain
variants.idiom_name: guard + goto FAIL_X into a reverse-order cleanup chain
variants.implementation_notes: CERT MEM12-C's second compliant solution: keep every guard an if but replace each return segment with a goto to the appropriate label in a single cleanup chain that unwinds resources in reverse acquisition order, so the function has one exit and the release order cannot drift between error paths. Choose it when the function owns three or more resources and per-guard cleanup would duplicate nested code; keep the plain early return when no resource is held at the guard point. CERT is explicit that the chain is a structured transfer within one function body, not general advocacy for goto.
pitfalls: A goto into a cleanup chain only works if the labels unwind in reverse acquisition order; inserting a resource without inserting its label releases in the wrong order or not at all.
The chain must not skip the initialisation of ret_val: every goto path needs a saved status before the jump, because errno is clobbered by the cleanup calls themselves.
